**أفضل حياً هادئاً** (ufaddil hayyan hadi'an) — both **حياً** and **هادئاً** are in the accusative (tanwin **-an**) because they are the object of **أفضل** (ufaddil, I prefer). The adjective agrees in case with the noun it modifies.

**ضائع** (da'i', lost) is the active participle of **ضاع** (da'a, to be lost) from root **ض-ي-ع** (d-y-', to be lost/wasted). **فاعل** pattern: one who is in a state of being lost.

**أنا ضائع** (ana da'i', I am lost) is a nominal sentence. The pronoun **أنا** (I) is the subject, **ضائع** (lost) is the predicate. No verb 'to be' is needed. To say 'I was lost' you would add **كنت**: **كنت ضائعاً** (kuntu da'i'an).

cards.english: I am a doctor. (أنا طبيب — no 'am')
cards.grammarNote:
State a job as a nominal sentence, with gender agreement:
**أنا طبيب** (male) / **أنا طبيبة** (female), **هو مهندس** (he's an engineer). The feminine adds **ة**: **مهندسة**.

Present-tense verbs change with a **prefix**: **أ** (I), **ت** (you/she), **ي** (he), **ن** (we):
**أعمل** (I work), **تعمل** (you work), **يعمل** (he works), **نعمل** (we work). The stem **-عمل-** stays the same.

Arabic profession nouns are masculine by default. Feminine is formed by adding **ة** (ta marbuta):
**طبيب** → **طبيبة** (tabib → tabiba = female doctor)
**مهندس** → **مهندسة** (muhandis → muhandisa = female engineer)
Unlike Spanish, no article is dropped: **أنا طبيب** (ana tabib) = I am a doctor.

**مُمَرِّض** (mumarriḍ, male nurse) / **مُمَرِّضة** (mumarriḍa, female nurse). From the root **م-ر-ض** (m-r-ḍ, illness/nursing). The **مُفَعِّل** (mufaʿʿil) pattern indicates someone who performs a repeated action — here, caring for the sick.
Broken plural: **مُمَرِّضون** (mumarriḍūn, male nurses), **مُمَرِّضات** (mumarriḍāt, female nurses).

**مُهَندِس** (muhandis) comes from the root **ه-ن-د-س** (h-n-d-s), borrowed from the Persian *handāzah* (measurement/geometry) via medieval Arabic. The **مُفَنعِل** pattern marks a practitioner.
Feminine: **مُهَندِسة** (muhandisa). Plural: **مُهَندِسون** (muhandisūn, m.) / **مُهَندِسات** (muhandisāt, f.).

**مُبَرمِج** (mubarmmij) from root **ب-ر-م-ج** (b-r-m-j) — a modern quadriliteral root derived from **برنامج** (barnāmaj, programme). The **مُفَعلِل** pattern on quadriliterals marks the agent/practitioner.
**أعمل كـ** (aʿmal ka-) = I work as. The prefix **كـ** (ka-) = as/like, attached directly to the following noun.

**طَاهٍ** (ṭāhin) is the active participle (**فَاعِل**) of the root **ط-ه-ي** (ṭ-h-y, to cook). The final ي drops before case endings, giving the tanwin form **طَاهٍ** (indefinite) or **الطَّاهِي** (definite).
Related: **مَطبَخ** (maṭbakh, kitchen) follows the **مَفعَل** place-pattern from root **ط-ب-خ** (ṭ-b-kh, to cook).
cards.englishPhrase: The cook works in the kitchen.

cards.grammarNote:
**نَادِل** (nādil, waiter) / **نَادِلة** (nādila, waitress). The **فَاعِل** pattern marks the doer — here, one who serves/calls.
**قَائِمة الطَّعَام** (qāʾimat aṭ-ṭaʿām) = menu, literally 'list of food' — an **إضافة** (iḍāfa) possessive chain. The definite article only appears on the second noun.

**مُدِير** (mudīr) from root **د-و-ر** (d-w-r, to turn/revolve/manage). Pattern **مُفعِل** = one who causes something. Feminine: **مُدِيرة** (mudīra). Plural: **مُدَراء** (mudarāʾ, broken plural) or **مُدِيرون** (mudīrūn).
Related: **إِدارة** (idāra, administration/management) from the same root.

**طَالِب** (ṭālib) = student, literally 'one who seeks/requests.' **فَاعِل** active participle from root **ط-ل-ب** (ṭ-l-b, to seek/request/demand). The same root gives **طَلَب** (ṭalab, request) and **مَطلوب** (maṭlūb, required/wanted).
Feminine: **طَالِبة** (ṭāliba). Plural: **طُلَّاب** (ṭullāb) or **طَالِبون** (ṭālibūn).

**مُهَندِس مِعمَارِي** = engineer + adjectival form of **عِمَارة** (ʿimāra, architecture/building). Root **ع-م-ر** (ʿ-m-r, to build/inhabit) also gives **عُمر** (ʿumr, lifespan) and **عَمَّار** (ʿammār, builder).
**مِعمَارِي** is the adjective: معماري literally means 'of construction/architecture.'

**مُحَامٍ** (muḥāmin) from root **ح-م-ي/و** (ḥ-m-y, to protect/defend). **مُفَاعِل** pattern = one who actively defends. Indefinite form ends in ـنٍ (the ي drops before case endings).
Feminine: **مُحَامِيَة** (muḥāmiya). The note **أختي** (ukhtī) = my sister — possessive suffix **ي** (-ī) attaches to the noun.

**رَاتِب** (rātib, salary) from root **ر-ت-ب** (r-t-b, to arrange/set in order). Literally 'something arranged/fixed regularly.' **رَتَّبَ** (rattaba, to arrange), **تَرتِيب** (tartīb, arrangement/order).
Phrasing: **ما هو الرَّاتِب؟** = What is the salary? Arabic question with **ما** (mā, what) + **هو** (huwa, it is) + definite noun.

**جَدوَل** (jadwal, schedule/table/river channel) — an interesting word with multiple meanings: originally 'a small stream,' then extended to 'a column/table/schedule.' Borrowed from Persian. Plural: **جَدَاوِل** (jadāwil — broken plural, pattern **فَعَاوِل**).
**مَرِن** (marin, flexible) from root **م-ر-ن** (m-r-n, to be supple/train).

**إِجَازة** (ijāza, vacation/permission/leave) — Form IV verbal noun from root **ج-و-ز** (j-w-z, to pass/allow). Originally means 'permission/authorization.' In Modern Arabic it covers both official leave and holiday travel.
**الأُسبُوع القَادِم** (al-usbūʿ al-qādim) = next week. **القَادِم** (qādim, coming/next) — **فَاعِل** of **ق-د-م** (q-d-m, to come/arrive).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going on vacation next week.

cards.grammarNote:
**اِسترَاحة** (istirāḥa, rest/break) — Form X verbal noun from root **ر-و-ح** (r-w-ḥ, to breathe/rest). Form X (**اِستَفعَلَ**) = to seek rest: **رَاحَ** (rāḥa, to rest/leave) → **اِسترَاحَ** (istirāḥa, to take a rest). Related: **رَاحة** (rāḥa, comfort), **رُوح** (rūḥ, soul/spirit — literally 'breath').
**لِنَأخُذ** (li-naʾkhudh) = let's take — cohortative **لِـ** + first-person plural.

**مَكتَب** (maktab, office/desk) — **مَفعَل** place-noun from root **ك-ت-ب** (k-t-b, to write). Literally 'the place of writing.' Same root: **كِتَاب** (book), **كِتَابة** (writing), **كَاتِب** (writer), **مَكتُوب** (letter/written thing).
This root family beautifully shows how Arabic patterns relate: مَفعَل = place where the verb action happens.

**زَمِيل** (zamīl, colleague/fellow) from root **ز-م-ل** (z-m-l, to accompany/wrap). **فَعِيل** adjective pattern often means 'sharing a quality.' **زُمَلاء** (zumalāʾ) is the broken plural — pattern **فُعَلاء**, typical for **فَعِيل** adjectives: **صَدِيق → أَصدِقاء**, **زَمِيل → زُمَلاء**.
**وَدُودون** (wadūdūn, friendly) — **فَعُول** intensive pattern from root **و-د-د** (w-d-d, to love).

**عَمِيل** (ʿamīl, customer/agent/client) from root **ع-م-ل** (ʿ-m-l, work/do). The **فَعِيل** pattern can mean 'one who does' or 'one done to.' Here it denotes someone who works with you (a client). Plural: **عُمَلاء** (ʿumalāʾ — broken plural **فُعَلاء**).
Do not confuse with **عَامِل** (ʿāmil, worker) which uses the **فَاعِل** pattern.

**فَرِيق** (farīq, team/group) from root **ف-ر-ق** (f-r-q, to separate/distinguish). Literally 'a separated/distinct group.' **فَرَّقَ** (farraqa, to divide), **فَارَقَ** (fāraqa, to part from), **فُرقَة** (furqa, separation/troupe), **فَرِيق** also means a military brigade.
Plural: **فِرَق** (firaq — broken plural, pattern **فِعَل**).
cards.englishPhrase: I work in a great team.

cards.grammarNote:
**مَشرُوع** (mashrūʿ, project/enterprise/lawful) — passive participle **مَفعُول** from root **ش-ر-ع** (sh-r-ʿ, to begin/legislate). Literally 'something undertaken/begun.' Also means 'lawful/permissible' in religious law: **غَير مَشرُوع** = unlawful. Plural: **مَشَارِيع** (mashārīʿ — broken plural **مَفَاعِيل**).
**شِبه مُنتَهٍ** = almost finished — **شِبه** (shabah, semi-/almost) + indefinite active participle.

**اِجتِمَاع** (ijtimāʿ, meeting/gathering) — Form VIII verbal noun from root **ج-م-ع** (j-m-ʿ, to gather/collect). Form VIII (**اِفتَعَلَ**) often has a reflexive sense: **جَمَعَ** (jamaʿa, to gather/bring together) → **اِجتَمَعَ** (ijtamaʿa, to gather together/meet). **مُجتَمَع** (mujtamaʿ, society) is from the same root and form.
cards.englishPhrase: We have a meeting at ten.

cards.grammarNote:
**وَقت فَرَاغ** (waqt farāgh, free time) = time of emptiness/vacancy. **فَرَاغ** (farāgh, emptiness/free space) from root **ف-ر-غ** (f-r-gh, to empty). **وَقت** (waqt, time) + **فَرَاغ** = an **إضافة** (iḍāfa) possessive chain without the definite article on the first noun.
**مَاذَا تَفعَل؟** (mādhā tafʿal?) = What do you do? **مَاذَا** = what (used before a verb), while **مَا** is used before a noun.
cards.englishPhrase: What do you do in your free time?

cards.english: I work in a hospital. (أعمل في / كـ)
cards.grammarNote:
**أعمل في** = I work in/at (a place); **أعمل كـ** = I work as (a role):
**أعمل في مستشفى** (I work in a hospital), **أعمل كطبيب** (I work as a doctor — **كـ** attaches to the word).

**يَعمَل** (yaʿmal, he works) from root **ع-م-ل** (ʿ-m-l, work/do) — one of the most productive roots in Arabic: **عَمَل** (ʿamal, work), **عَامِل** (ʿāmil, worker — **فَاعِل**), **مَعمَل** (maʿmal, laboratory/workshop — **مَفعَل** place pattern), **عَمَلِيَّة** (ʿamaliyya, operation/process).
**مُستَشفَى** (mustashfā, hospital) from root **ش-ف-ي** (sh-f-y, to heal): **شِفَاء** (shifāʾ, cure), **Form X** = place where healing is sought.

**القِرَاءَة** (al-qirāʾa, reading) is a verbal noun (مَصدَر, maṣdar) from root **ق-ر-أ** (q-r-ʾ, to read). The same root gives **قُرآن** (Qurʾān, the recitation) and **قَارِئ** (qāriʾ, reader — **فَاعِل** pattern).
Verbal nouns in Arabic function like gerunds: أُحِبُّ القِراءَة = I love reading (the reading).

**الكِتَابَة** (al-kitāba, writing) — verbal noun (مَصدَر) from root **ك-ت-ب** (k-t-b, to write). This root is one of the most productive in Arabic: **كِتَاب** (kitāb, book), **كَاتِب** (kātib, writer — **فَاعِل**), **مَكتَب** (maktab, office/desk — **مَفعَل** place pattern), **مَكتوب** (maktūb, written/letter).

**الرَّسم** (ar-rasm) = drawing/painting/sketching. From root **ر-س-م** (r-s-m, to draw/sketch). **رَسَّام** (rassām, artist/painter — intensive **فَعَّال** pattern). **رُسُوم** (rusūm, drawings, broken plural).
**الرَّسم** is a sun-letter word: **الـ** assimilates to **ر**, so it is pronounced *ar-rasm*, not *al-rasm*.

**الرَّسم** (ar-rasm) serves as both 'drawing' and 'painting' in Arabic — the same verbal noun covers both. From root **ر-س-م** (r-s-m, to draw/sketch/inscribe). The sun letter **ر** assimilates the definite article: *al-rasm* → *ar-rasm*.
Distinguish **رَسم** (rasm, drawing/sketch) from **لَوحَة** (lawḥa, a painted artwork/canvas).

**المُوسِيقَى** (al-mūsīqā) is a loanword from Greek *mousikē* (the art of the Muses), entering Arabic via Greek and Syriac. It is one of many scientific/artistic terms borrowed into Arabic during the Abbasid translation movement (8th–10th c.).
**أَستَمِع إلى** (astamīʿ ilā) = I listen to. Root **س-م-ع** (s-m-ʿ, to hear); Form X **اِستَمَعَ** = to listen attentively.
cards.englishPhrase: I listen to music every day.

cards.grammarNote:
**الغِنَاء** (al-ghinā', singing) — verbal noun from root **غ-ن-ي** (gh-n-y, to sing/be self-sufficient). **غَنَّى** (ghannā, to sing — Form II intensive), **مُغَنٍّ** (mughanin, singer — Form II active participle, drops ي before case endings).
**أُغنِيَة** (ughniya, song) from the same root; plural **أَغَانٍ** (aghānin — broken plural). Note the moon letter **غ**: the article stays *al-ghinā'*, not assimilated.

**العَزف** (al-ʿazf, playing an instrument) from root **ع-ز-ف** (ʿ-z-f, to play a musical instrument). **عَزَفَ على** (ʿazafa ʿalā) = to play [instrument]. **آلة مُوسِيقِيَّة** (āla mūsīqiyya) = musical instrument — **آلة** (āla, tool/instrument) + **مُوسِيقِيَّة** (nisba adjective).
**الغِيتَار** (al-ghītār) is a loanword from Spanish *guitarra* / English 'guitar'.

**الرَّقص** (ar-raqṣ, dancing) from root **ر-ق-ص** (r-q-ṣ, to dance/jump). Sun letter **ر** causes assimilation: *ar-raqṣ*.
**رَاقِص** (rāqiṣ, dancer — **فَاعِل**), **رَاقِصة** (rāqiṣa, female dancer). Plural of the verbal noun is uncommon; you say **رُقصَة** (raqṣa) for a single dance.

**الطَّبخ** (aṭ-ṭabkh, cooking) from root **ط-ب-خ** (ṭ-b-kh, to cook). Sun letter **ط** causes assimilation.
**طَبَخَ** (ṭabakha, to cook), **طَاهٍ** (ṭāhin, cook — **فَاعِل**), **مَطبَخ** (maṭbakh, kitchen — **مَفعَل** place pattern).
**أستمتع بـ** (astamtiʿ bi-) = I enjoy. Root **م-ت-ع** (m-t-ʿ, pleasure), Form X with **بـ** preposition.

**المَشي** (al-mashī, walking) — verbal noun from root **م-ش-ي** (m-sh-y, to walk). **لِمَسَافَات طَوِيلة** (li-masāfāt ṭawīla) = for long distances. **مَسَافة** (masāfa, distance) from root **س-و-ف** (s-w-f), plural **مَسَافات** (sound feminine plural).
**الجِبَال** (al-jibāl, mountains) is the broken plural of **جَبَل** (jabal, mountain) — pattern **فِعَال**.
cards.englishPhrase: I like hiking in the mountains.

cards.grammarNote:
**الجَري** (al-jarī, running) — verbal noun from root **ج-ر-ي** (j-r-y, to run/flow). Related: **مَجرَى** (majrā, course/channel — **مَفعَل** pattern), **جَارٍ** (jārin, running/flowing — **فَاعِل**). The phrase uses **أَركُض** (arkuḍ, I run) from root **ر-ك-ض** (r-k-ḍ) — a near-synonym for running.
Both roots are used: **جَرَى** (to run/flow, often metaphorical), **رَكَضَ** (to run, physical movement).

For hobbies, use **أحب** + the **verbal noun** (the 'act of…'), usually with **الـ**:
**أحب السباحة** (I like swimming), **أحب القراءة** (I like reading), **أحب الجري** (I like running).

**السِّبَاحة** (as-sibāḥa, swimming) from root **س-ب-ح** (s-b-ḥ, to swim/glorify God). The same root gives **سُبحَانَ الله** (subḥāna allāh, 'glory be to God') — a beautiful polysemy. **سَبَّاح** (sabbāḥ, swimmer — intensive **فَعَّال** pattern).
**السِّبَاحة** is a sun-letter word: pronounced *as-sibāḥa*.

**رُكُوب الدَّرَّاجة** (rukūb ad-darrāja) = riding the bicycle — an **إضافة** (iḍāfa) possessive chain: verbal noun + definite noun. **رُكُوب** (rukūb, riding) — verbal noun from root **ر-ك-ب** (r-k-b, to ride/mount). **رَاكِب** (rākib, rider — **فَاعِل**), **مَركَبة** (markaba, vehicle).
**الدَّرَّاجة** (ad-darrāja, bicycle) from root **د-ر-ج** (d-r-j, to go in steps/roll) — sun letter **د** causes assimilation.
cards.phrase: أركب الدراجة في عطلة نهاية الأسبوع.

cards.grammarNote:
**السَّفَر** (as-safar, travel) from root **س-ف-ر** (s-f-r, to travel/reveal). Related: **سَفِير** (safīr, ambassador — literally 'one who travels/mediates'), **سِفَارة** (sifāra, embassy). The English word 'safari' (through Swahili) traces back to this same Arabic root.
**أُحِبُّ السَّفَر** — a definite verbal noun used as a direct object.

**أَلعَاب الفِيدِيو** (alʿāb al-fīdyū) = video games. **أَلعَاب** is the broken plural of **لُعبَة** (luʿba, game) — pattern **أَفعَال**. Root **ل-ع-ب** (l-ʿ-b, to play): **يَلعَب** (yalʿab, he plays), **لَاعِب** (lāʿib, player — **فَاعِل**).
**الفِيدِيو** is a loanword from English 'video'.
cards.englishPhrase: He plays video games at night.
cards.phrase: هو يلعب ألعاب الفيديو في الليل.
cards.phraseRomanized: huwa yal'ab al'ab al-vidyu fi al-layl.

cards.grammarNote:
**مُشَاهَدة** (mushāhada, watching) — Form III verbal noun from root **ش-ه-د** (sh-h-d, to witness/see). Form III implies reciprocity: **شَاهَدَ** (shāhada, to watch/view). Related: **شَاهِد** (shāhid, witness), **مَشهَد** (mashhad, scene/sight — place noun).
**التِّلفَاز** (at-tilfāz, television) — loanword from Latin/Greek via French *télévision*, Arabized. Sun letter **ت** causes assimilation. Colloquial: **تلفزيون** (tilfiziyūn).

**الاِستِمَاع** (al-istimāʿ, listening) — Form X verbal noun from root **س-م-ع** (s-m-ʿ, to hear). Form X (**اِستَفعَلَ**) adds intention/effort: **سَمِعَ** (samiʿa, to hear passively) vs. **اِستَمَعَ** (istamaʿa, to listen actively/attentively). Always followed by **إلى** (ilā, to): **اِستَمَعَ إلى** = to listen to.
Compare: **سَمِعَ** (heard) — passive; **اِستَمَعَ** (listened) — deliberate.

**التَّمرِين** (at-tamrīn, exercise/training) from root **م-ر-ن** (m-r-n, to be supple/practise). Form II verbal noun pattern **تَفعِيل**.
**الصَّالة الرِّيَاضِيَّة** (aṣ-ṣāla ar-riyāḍiyya, sports hall/gym) — **رِيَاضة** (riyāḍa, sport) from root **ر-و-ض** (r-w-ḍ, to tame/cultivate). **رِيَاضِيَّة** is the adjectival form (nisba adjective with **ـِيَّة** suffix).
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the gym for exercise.

cards.grammarNote: **الهَوَاء الطَّلق** (al-hawāʾ aṭ-ṭalq) = the open air, literally 'the free/unrestrained air.' **هَوَاء** (hawāʾ, air) from root **ه-و-ي** (h-w-y, to blow/love). **طَلق** (ṭalq, free/open) from root **ط-ل-ق** (ṭ-l-q, to release/free). Note sun-letter assimilation: **الط** → *aṭ-ṭalq*.

**مُبدِع** (mubdiʿ, creative) — Form IV active participle of root **ب-د-ع** (b-d-ʿ, to create/innovate). **أَبدَعَ** (abdaʿa, to create/excel), **إِبدَاع** (ibdāʿ, creativity/innovation — Form IV verbal noun), **بَدِيع** (badīʿ, wondrous/original — adjective, also a name).
Feminine: **مُبدِعَة** (mubdiʿa). The **جِداً** (jiddan, very) comes after the predicate adjective.

**مُثِير لِلاِهتِمَام** (muthīr lil-ihtimām) = interesting, literally 'arousing/exciting for attention.' **مُثِير** (muthīr, arousing — Form IV active participle of **ث-و-ر**, to stir up). **اِهتِمَام** (ihtimām, attention/interest — Form VIII verbal noun from root **ه-م-م**, to concern/care).
This is a very common compound adjective in Modern Standard Arabic.

**مُمِلّ** (mumill, boring/tedious) — Form IV active participle of root **م-ل-ل** (m-l-l, to be bored/weary). **مَلَل** (malal, boredom), **مَلَّ** (malla, to be bored). Pattern **مُفعِل** = 'that which causes' the state: **مُمِلّ** = 'that which causes boredom.'
**كَانَ مُمِلاً** = was boring: **كَانَ** (kāna, was) + adjective in the accusative (مُمِلاً with tanwin **ـاً**).

**يَتَقَاضَى** (yataqāḍā, he earns/collects a salary) — Form VI of root **ق-ض-ي** (q-ḍ-y, to judge/fulfil/collect a debt). Form VI implies mutual action or gradual fulfilment: **قَضَى** (qaḍā, to fulfil/spend time) → **تَقَاضَى** (taqāḍā, to receive/collect what is owed).
**رَاتِباً جَيِّداً** — both words end in **ـاً** (tanwin accusative): **رَاتِب** (salary) as direct object + **جَيِّد** (good) as adjective, both indefinite accusative.

**يَتَقَاعَد** (yataqāʿad, he retires) — Form VI of root **ق-ع-د** (q-ʿ-d, to sit/stay). Form VI implies mutual withdrawal or gradual stepping back: **قَعَدَ** (qaʿada, to sit/remain) → **تَقَاعَدَ** (taqāʿada, to retire/withdraw). **التَّقَاعُد** (at-taqāʿud) = retirement (verbal noun).
**العَام المَاضِي** = last year — **مَاضٍ** (māḍin, past/last) from root **م-ض-ي** (m-ḍ-y, to pass).

**وَظِيفة** (waẓīfa, job/function/duty) from root **و-ظ-ف** (w-ẓ-f, to assign a task). **فَعِيلة** pattern. **وَظَّفَ** (waẓẓafa, to employ — Form II), **مُوَظَّف** (muwaẓẓaf, employee — Form II passive participle). Plural: **وَظَائِف** (waẓāʾif — broken plural **فَعَائِل**).
Note: **وَظِيفة** (waẓīfa) = formal job/post, while **عَمَل** (ʿamal) = work in general. Use **وَظِيفة** for an official position.

**عَاطِل عَن العَمَل** (ʿāṭil ʿan al-ʿamal) = idle/away from work. **عَاطِل** (ʿāṭil, idle — **فَاعِل**) from root **ع-ط-ل** (ʿ-ṭ-l, to be idle/unemployed). The preposition **عَن** (ʿan, away from) completes the meaning. Literally 'one who is idle from work.'
Modern alternative: **بِدُون عَمَل** (bidūn ʿamal) = without work. Colloquially: **عَاطِل** alone is widely understood.

**يَدرُس** (yadrus, he studies) from root **د-ر-س** (d-r-s, to study/tread a path). Related: **دَرس** (dars, lesson), **دِرَاسة** (dirāsa, study/studies — verbal noun Form I), **مَدرَسة** (madrasa, school — **مَفعَلة** place pattern), **مُدَرِّس** (mudarris, teacher — Form II active participle).

**يَتَعَلَّم** (yataʿallam, he learns) — Form V of root **ع-ل-م** (ʿ-l-m, knowledge). Form V (**تَفَعَّلَ**) of Form II often means 'to acquire' the state: **عَلَّمَ** (ʿallama, to teach) → **تَعَلَّمَ** (taʿallama, to learn). Same root: **عِلم** (ʿilm, science/knowledge), **عَالِم** (ʿālim, scholar), **مَعلُومة** (maʿlūma, information), **عَالَم** (ʿālam, world).

**يَتَدَرَّب** (yatadarrab, he practices/trains) — Form V of root **د-ر-ب** (d-r-b, to train/accustom). **دَرَّبَ** (darraba, to train sb.) → **تَدَرَّبَ** (tadarraba, to train oneself/practice). Related: **تَدرِيب** (tadrīb, training), **مُدَرِّب** (mudarrib, trainer/coach).

**يُدَرِّس** (yudarris, he teaches) — Form II of root **د-ر-س** (d-r-s, to study). Form II doubles the middle radical and usually gives a causative or intensive meaning: **دَرَسَ** (darasa, to study) → **دَرَّسَ** (darrasa, to teach). Compare: **كَتَبَ** (to write) → **كَتَّبَ** (to make write), **عَلِمَ** (to know) → **عَلَّمَ** (to teach).

**يَبنِي** (yabnī, he builds) from root **ب-ن-ي** (b-n-y, to build). Related: **بِنَاء** (binā', building/construction), **مَبنَى** (mabnā, building/structure — **مَفعَل** pattern), **بَنِيَّة** (baniyya, structure).
**مَدرَسة** (madrasa, school) is a **مَفعَلة** place-noun from **د-ر-س** (to study) — where studying happens.
cards.englishPhrase: They are building a new school.

cards.grammarNote:
**يُصلِح** (yuṣliḥ, he fixes) — Form IV of root **ص-ل-ح** (ṣ-l-ḥ, to be good/sound). Form IV (**أَفعَلَ**) = causative: **صَلَحَ** (ṣalaḥa, to be sound/good) → **أَصلَحَ** (aṣlaḥa, to fix/reform). **إِصلَاح** (iṣlāḥ, repair/reform — Form IV verbal noun), **إِصلَاحَات** (iṣlāḥāt, reforms).
Related: **مُصلِح** (muṣliḥ, reformer), **صُلح** (ṣulḥ, peace/reconciliation).

**يَصنَع** (yaṣnaʿ, he makes/manufactures) from root **ص-ن-ع** (ṣ-n-ʿ, to make). **صَنَاعة** (ṣanāʿa, industry/craft), **صَانِع** (ṣāniʿ, maker — **فَاعِل**), **مَصنَع** (maṣnaʿ, factory — **مَفعَل** place pattern).
**القَهوَة** (al-qahwa, coffee) — a word Arabic gave to the world: English 'coffee', Turkish *kahve*, French *café* all come from this Arabic source.

**يُصَمِّم** (yuṣammim, he designs) — Form II of root **ص-م-م** (ṣ-m-m, to be firm/decide/design). **تَصمِيم** (taṣmīm, design — Form II verbal noun), **مُصَمِّم** (muṣammim, designer — Form II active participle).
**مَوَاقِع** (mawāqiʿ) is the broken plural of **مَوقِع** (mawqiʿ, site/location) — pattern **مَفَاعِل**.

**يَبِيع** (yabīʿ, he sells) from root **ب-ي-ع** (b-y-ʿ, to sell/trade). **بَيع** (bayʿ, sale), **بَائِع** (bāʾiʿ, seller — **فَاعِل**), **مَبِيع** (mabīʿ, sold item — **مَفعُول** pattern).
**السَّيَّارَات** (as-sayyārāt) = cars, sound feminine plural of **سَيَّارة** (sayyāra) — from root **س-ي-ر** (s-y-r, to travel).

**يَشتَرِي** (yashtarī, he buys) — Form VIII of root **ش-ر-ي** (sh-r-y, to buy/sell). Form VIII (**اِفتَعَلَ**) here adds a nuance of mutual exchange. **شِرَاء** (shirāʾ, purchase — verbal noun), **مُشتَرٍ** (mushtarin, buyer).
**حَاسُوب** (ḥāsūb, computer) from root **ح-س-ب** (ḥ-s-b, to calculate) — literally 'that which calculates.'
cards.englishPhrase: I need to buy a new computer.

cards.grammarNote: **يُسَاعِد** (yusāʿid, he helps) — Form III of root **س-ع-د** (s-ʿ-d, to be happy/assist). Form III (**فَاعَلَ**) often implies reciprocity or helping toward a goal: **سَعَدَ** (saʿada, to be happy) → **سَاعَدَ** (sāʿada, to assist). **مُسَاعَدة** (musāʿada, help/assistance — Form III verbal noun).

**يُدِير** (yudīr, he manages/directs) — Form IV of root **د-و-ر** (d-w-r, to turn/revolve). Form IV: **أَدَارَ** (adāra, to manage/run). **إِدَارة** (idāra, management/administration — Form IV verbal noun), **مُدِير** (mudīr, manager — Form IV active participle).
The root conveys rotation/running: **دَوْرة** (dawra, cycle/turn), **دَوَام** (dawām, continuity/permanence at work).

**يَجتَمِع** (yajtamiʿ, he meets/gathers) — Form VIII of root **ج-م-ع** (j-m-ʿ, to gather). Form VIII (**اِفتَعَلَ**) is reflexive: **جَمَعَ** (jamaʿa, to gather people) → **اِجتَمَعَ** (ijtamaʿa, to gather oneself/meet together). **مُجتَمَع** (mujtamaʿ, society — the place of gathering).
Note: **قَابَلَ** (qābala, Form III) = to meet one-on-one; **اِجتَمَعَ** = to meet as a group.

**يَبدَأ** (yabdaʾ, he starts) from root **ب-د-أ** (b-d-ʾ, to begin). **بِدَايَة** (bidāya, beginning), **مَبدَأ** (mabdaʾ, principle — **مَفعَل** pattern, literally 'the starting point').
**في الثَّامِنة** (fi ath-thāmina) = at eight (o'clock). Arabic uses the feminine ordinal: **الثَّامِنة** = the eighth (hour). The definite article assimilates: **الث** → pronounced *ath-thāmina* (sun letter ث).

**يُنهِي** (yunhī, he finishes) — Form IV of root **ن-ه-ي** (n-h-y, to end/forbid). Form IV (**أَفعَلَ**) = causative: **نَهَى** (nahā, to forbid/come to end) → **أَنهَى** (anhā, to finish/conclude). Related: **نِهَاية** (nihāya, end/conclusion), **مُنتَهٍ** (muntahin, finished — Form VIII active participle).

**يحب** (yuhibb) = to love / like — the subject is always the person, not the thing liked.
**أحب القراءة** (uhibb al-qira'a) = I like reading.
**هي تحب الغناء** (hiya tuhibb al-ghina') = she likes singing.
cards.englishPhrase: I like reading. She likes singing.

cards.grammarNote: **يَستَرخِي** (yastarkhi, he relaxes) — Form X of root **ر-خ-و/ي** (r-kh-w, to be loose/relaxed). Form X (**اِستَفعَلَ**) = to become or seek a state: **رَخَا** (rakhā, to be loose) → **اِستَرخَى** (istarkha, to relax/become loose). **اِسترَاحة** (istirāḥa, rest/break) is related from the same Form X idea.

**مُجهِد** (mujhid, exhausting/stressful) — Form IV active participle of root **ج-ه-د** (j-h-d, to exert effort/strive). **جَهد** (jahd, effort), **جِهَاد** (jihād, striving/struggle), **مَجهُود** (majhūd, exerted effort). The pattern **مُفعِل** marks 'the one causing' the root action — so **مُجهِد** = 'that which causes exhaustion.'

Feelings are nominal sentences (no 'am'), and the adjective agrees in gender:
**أنا سعيد** (male) / **أنا سعيدة** (female) = I'm happy, **أنا حزين / حزينة** (I'm sad).

**أشعر بـ** (ash'ur bi-) = I feel + (a noun); **بـ** attaches to the following word:
**أشعر بالتعب** (I feel tired[ness]), **أشعر بالسعادة** (I feel happy[ness]), **أشعر بالخوف** (I feel fear).

Arabic adjectives agree in gender: **سعيد** (sa'id, m.) / **سعيدة** (sa'ida, f.).
They also agree in definiteness when modifying a noun:
**رجل سعيد** (a happy man) vs. **الرجل السعيد** (the happy man).
In predicate position ('I am happy'), the adjective stays indefinite: **أنا سعيد** (ana sa'id).

**حَزِين** (ḥazīn, sad) — **فَعِيل** adjective pattern from root **ح-ز-ن** (ḥ-z-n, to be sad). **حَزِنَ** (ḥazina, to be sad), **حُزن** (ḥuzn, sadness — noun), **حَزَن** (ḥazan, grief). The **فَعِيل** pattern often describes a lasting state or quality.
Feminine: **حَزِينة** (ḥazīna). Plural: **حُزَنَاء** (ḥuzanāʾ — broken plural **فُعَلاء**).

**حُبّ** (ḥubb, love) from root **ح-ب-ب** (ḥ-b-b, to love). **أَحَبَّ** (aḥabba, to love — Form IV), **حَبِيب** (ḥabīb, beloved/darling — **فَعِيل** pattern), **مَحبُوب** (maḥbūb, loved one — passive participle), **مَحَبَّة** (maḥabba, affection/love).
**أَشعُر بِحُبٍّ** = I feel love — note the **بـ** (bi-) preposition: شَعَرَ بـ = to feel [noun].
cards.englishPhrase: I feel a lot of love for my family.

cards.grammarNote:
**غَضَب** (ghaḍab, anger) from root **غ-ض-ب** (gh-ḍ-b, to be angry). **غَضِبَ** (ghaḍiba, to become angry — stative Form I), **غَاضِب** (ghāḍib, angry — **فَاعِل** active participle), **غَضبَان** (ghaḍbān, furious — **فَعلَان** intensive adjective for emotional states).
**شَعَرتُ بِالغَضَب** = I felt anger — definite noun after بـ.
cards.englishPhrase: I felt anger when they lied to me.

cards.grammarNote:
**خَوف** (khawf, fear) from root **خ-و-ف** (kh-w-f, to fear). **خَافَ** (khāfa, to be afraid — Form I with a middle weak root), **خَائِف** (khāʾif, afraid — **فَاعِل**), **خَوَّافة** (khawwāfa, cowardly — intensive **فَعَّال**).
**أَنَا خَائِف مِن الظَّلَام** — note the definite article on **الظَّلَام** (aẓ-ẓalām, the dark) — sun letter **ظ**.

**أَمَل** (amal, hope) from root **أ-م-ل** (ʾ-m-l, to hope/expect). **أَمَّلَ** (ammala, to give hope — Form II), **تَأَمَّلَ** (taʾammala, to contemplate/meditate — Form V), **مُؤَمِّل** (muʾammil, one who hopes).
**المُستَقبَل** (al-mustaqbal, the future) from root **ق-ب-ل** (q-b-l, to receive/accept) — Form X: 'the time that will be received ahead.'
cards.englishPhrase: I have hope for the future.

cards.grammarNote: **ضَغط** (ḍaghṭ, pressure/stress) from root **ض-غ-ط** (ḍ-gh-ṭ, to press/squeeze). **ضَغَطَ** (ḍaghaṭa, to press), **ضَغط الدَّم** (ḍaghṭ ad-dam, blood pressure). In Modern Arabic, **ضَغط** covers both physical pressure and psychological stress/pressure at work.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of stress at work.

cards.grammarNote:
**مِزَاج** (mizāj, mood/temperament) from root **م-ز-ج** (m-z-j, to mix/blend). In classical medicine, *mizāj* referred to one's bodily constitution — the blend of the four humors. The medieval Arabic medical tradition (Ibn Sina/Avicenna) used this concept; European medicine adopted it as 'temperament.'
**مِزَاجِي جَيِّد** = my mood is good (equational sentence — no verb 'to be').
cards.englishPhrase: I'm in a good mood today.

cards.grammarNote:
**شُعُور** (shuʿūr, feeling/awareness) — verbal noun from root **ش-ع-ر** (sh-ʿ-r, to feel/perceive/know). **شَعَرَ** (shaʿara, to feel), **شِعر** (shiʿr, poetry — originally 'to be aware of beauty'), **شَاعِر** (shāʿir, poet — **فَاعِل**). The link between feeling and poetry is embedded in the root.
**طَبِيعِيّ** (ṭabīʿī, natural/normal) from root **ط-ب-ع** (ṭ-b-ʿ, nature/print).

**عَاطِفة** (ʿāṭifa, emotion/feeling/sentiment) — **فَاعِلة** feminine active participle from root **ع-ط-ف** (ʿ-ṭ-f, to bend toward/show affection). Plural: **عَوَاطِف** (ʿawāṭif — broken plural **فَوَاعِل**).
**لَم أَستَطِع** (lam astaṭiʿ, I could not) — **لَم** negates the past with a present-tense verb (jussive mood). Root **ط-و-ع** (ṭ-w-ʿ, to obey/be able), Form X.

**هُدُوء** (hudūʾ, calm/tranquility) from root **ه-د-أ** (h-d-ʾ, to calm down/be still). **هَدَأَ** (hadaʾa, to calm down), **هَادِئ** (hādiʾ, calm — **فَاعِل**), **تَهدِئَة** (tahdiʾa, calming/pacification — Form II verbal noun).
Note: **هُدُوئِك** (hudūʾik) = your calm — possessive suffix **كِ** (ki, your, f.) attached to the noun.

**قَلَق** (qalaq, anxiety/worry) from root **ق-ل-ق** (q-l-q, to be restless/agitated). Reduplicated root. **قَلِقَ** (qaliqa, to be anxious), **قَلِق** (qaliq, anxious/worried — **فَعِل** stative pattern). In Modern Arabic **قَلَق** is widely used for both worry and existential anxiety.
Note: this is both the noun **قَلَق** and the adjective **قَلِق** — different vowels, same root.

**مُفَاجَأة** (mufājaʾa, surprise) — Form III verbal noun from root **ف-ج-أ** (f-j-ʾ, to come suddenly). **فَجَأَةً** (fajʾatan, suddenly — adverb), **فَاجَأَ** (fājaʾa, to surprise/take by surprise). Plural: **مُفَاجَآت** (mufājaʾāt, surprises — sound feminine plural).
**يَا لَهُ مِن مُفَاجَأَة!** = what a surprise! — the Arabic exclamation formula (see: يا له من...).

**كُره** (kurh, hate/hatred) from root **ك-ر-ه** (k-r-h, to hate/dislike). **كَرِهَ** (kariha, to hate — Form I stative), **كَرَاهِيَة** (karāhiyya, hatred — a longer verbal noun), **مَكرُوه** (makrūh, disliked — passive participle, also a religious term for a discouraged but not forbidden act).
Note the short form **كُره** (kurh) vs. the longer noun **كَرَاهِيَة** (karāhiyya) — both mean hatred.

**أَلَم** (alam, pain) from root **أ-ل-م** (ʾ-l-m, to hurt/pain). **أَلِمَ** (alima, to be in pain), **أَلِيم** (alīm, painful — **فَعِيل**), **مُؤلِم** (muʾlim, causing pain — Form IV active participle), **مُؤلِمة** (muʾlima, painful, feminine).
**سَاقِي** (sāqī) = my leg — possessive suffix **ي** (-ī) on **سَاق** (sāq, leg).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel pain in my leg.

cards.grammarNote:
**طَاقَة** (ṭāqa, energy/capacity) from root **ط-و-ق** (ṭ-w-q, to be able/to encircle). **أَطَاقَ** (aṭāqa, to be capable of — Form IV), **طَاقَة** literally means 'capability/capacity,' extended in Modern Arabic to physical and electrical energy.
**لَدَيَّ طَاقَة كَثِيرة** — indefinite noun in subject position of equational sentence after لدي.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of energy today.

cards.grammarNote:
**يَشعُر** (yashʿur, he feels) from root **ش-ع-ر** (sh-ʿ-r, to perceive/feel). Always used with **بـ** (bi-) when expressing a feeling: **شَعَرَ بِـ** = to feel [noun].
**أَشعُر بِخَير** (ashʿur bi-khayr) = I feel well/good. **خَير** (khayr, good/well-being) from root **خ-ي-ر** (kh-y-r, good). Note: you cannot say *أشعر خيراً* — the بـ is obligatory.

**يُحِبّ** (yuḥibb, he loves) — Form IV of root **ح-ب-ب** (ḥ-b-b, to love). Form IV (**أَفعَلَ**) here is the active form. **أَحَبَّ** (aḥabba, to love), **حَبِيب** (ḥabīb, beloved — **فَعِيل**), **حُبّ** (ḥubb, love — noun).
**أُحِبُّكَ** (uḥibbuka) = I love you (m.) / **أُحِبُّكِ** (uḥibbuki) = I love you (f.) — gender matters in the suffix.

**يَكرَه** (yakrahu, he hates) from root **ك-ر-ه** (k-r-h, to hate/find repugnant). Form I stative verb.
**أَكرَهُ الاِنتِظَار** = I hate waiting. The verbal noun **الاِنتِظَار** (al-intiẓār, the waiting) acts as the direct object — like a gerund in English. From root **ن-ظ-ر** (n-ẓ-r, to look/wait), Form VIII: 'to look/wait with expectation.'

Arabic uses the same verb **يُحِبّ** (yuḥibb) for both 'to love' and 'to like' — context and degree make the distinction. When followed by a definite noun (with الـ), it reads as liking: **أُحِبُّ المُوسِيقَى** = I like music. When followed by a person, it can mean love.
Compare: **أُحِبُّ المُوسِيقَى** (I like music) vs. **أُحِبُّكِ** (I love you).

**يَستَمتِع** (yastamtiʿ, he enjoys) — Form X of root **م-ت-ع** (m-t-ʿ, to enjoy/provide pleasure). Form X (**اِستَفعَلَ**) = to seek or acquire the root quality: **مَتَّعَ** (mattaʿa, to give enjoyment) → **اِستَمتَعَ** (istamtaʿa, to enjoy for oneself). Always followed by **بـ** (bi-): **اِستَمتَعَ بـ** = to enjoy [something].

**يَخشَى** (yakhshā, he fears) from root **خ-ش-ي** (kh-sh-y, to fear/dread — a stronger fear than خاف). **خَشِيَ** (khashiya, to dread/fear), **خَشيَة** (khashya, dread/reverence), **خَاشِع** (khāshiʿ, humble/reverent).
The difference: **خَافَ** = general fear; **خَشِيَ** = a deeper, reverential fear — used for fearing God as well as profound dread.

**يَأمُل** (yaʾmul, he hopes) from root **أ-م-ل** (ʾ-m-l, to hope/expect). **آمُل أَن** (āmulu an, I hope that) + subjunctive verb.
**عَلَى مَا يُرَام** (ʿalā mā yurām) = as desired/well — a fixed Arabic expression, literally 'upon what is wished.' **يُرَام** is passive present of **رَامَ** (to desire). The whole phrase means 'perfectly, all is well.'
cards.phrase: آمل أن يسير كل شيء على ما يرام.
cards.phraseRomanized: amal an yasir kull shay' 'ala ma yuram.

cards.grammarNote:
**يَقلَق** (yaqlaqu, he worries) from root **ق-ل-ق** (q-l-q, to be restless). **لَا تَقلَق** (lā taqlaqu) = don't worry — **لَا** + present tense verb = prohibition.
**بِشَأنِ** (bi-shaʾni) = regarding/about — a preposition phrase. **شَأن** (shaʾn, matter/affair/concern) from root **ش-أ-ن** (sh-ʾ-n). Compare with **بِخُصوص** (bi-khuṣūṣ, regarding) — both are common.

**سَلَام** (salām, peace/safety/greeting) from root **س-ل-م** (s-l-m, to be safe/submit). One of the most important roots in Arabic: **إِسلَام** (Islam, submission/peace), **مُسلِم** (Muslim, one who submits), **سَلَّمَ** (sallama, to greet/hand over), **سَلَامة** (salāma, safety).
The greeting **السَّلَام عَلَيكُم** (as-salāmu ʿalaykum) = peace be upon you.

**غَيرَة** (ghayra, jealousy/protective zeal) from root **غ-ي-ر** (gh-y-r, to change/be jealous). In Arabic culture, **غَيرَة** can be positive (protecting what is precious) or negative (destructive jealousy). Contrast with **حَسَد** (ḥasad, envy of another's good fortune).
**قَد تُدَمِّر** (qad tudammir) = can destroy / may destroy — **قَد** before a present-tense verb expresses possibility. **عَلَاقَات** (ʿalāqāt) = relationships (sound feminine plural of **عَلَاقة**).

**يُزعِج** (yuzʿij, he annoys/disturbs) — Form IV of root **ز-ع-ج** (z-ʿ-j, to disturb/unsettle). Form IV = causative: **زَعِجَ** (zaʿija, to be disturbed) → **أَزعَجَ** (azʿaja, to annoy/disturb someone). **إِزعَاج** (izʿāj, annoyance — Form IV verbal noun).
The suffix **ـني** (-nī) = me: **يُزعِجني** = it annoys me. Object pronoun suffixes attach directly to the verb.

**يُغضِب** (yughḍib, he angers/makes angry) — Form IV of root **غ-ض-ب** (gh-ḍ-b, to be angry). Form IV = causative: **غَضِبَ** (ghaḍiba, to become angry) → **أَغضَبَ** (aghḍaba, to make angry). **أَغضَبَني** (aghḍabanī) = angered me — note **ـني** suffix.
Compare the family: **غَضَب** (noun: anger), **غَضبَان** (adj: furious — **فَعلَان** emotional pattern), **غَاضِب** (adj: angry — **فَاعِل**), **يُغضِب** (verb: to anger).

**يَبتَسِم** (yabtasim, he smiles) — Form VIII of root **ب-س-م** (b-s-m, to smile). Form VIII (**اِفتَعَلَ**) here intensifies the action slightly: **بَسَمَ** (basama, to smile gently) → **اِبتَسَمَ** (ibtasama, to smile). **اِبتِسَامة** (ibtisāma, a smile — Form VIII verbal noun).
**دَائِماً** (dāʾiman, always) — accusative adverb from **دَوَام** (dawām, continuity), root **د-و-م** (d-w-m, to be permanent).

**يَضحَك** (yaḍḥak, he laughs) from root **ض-ح-ك** (ḍ-ḥ-k, to laugh). **ضَحِكَ** (ḍaḥika, to laugh — Form I), **ضَحكَة** (ḍaḥka, a laugh), **ضَحَّاك** (ḍaḥḥāk, someone who laughs a lot — **فَعَّال** intensive). Note: **ضَحِكَ على** (ḍaḥika ʿalā) = to laugh *at* someone (mocking); **ضَحِكَ مع** = to laugh *with*.
**ضَحِكنَا** (ḍaḥiknā) = we laughed — the suffix **ـنَا** (-nā) = we (past tense).

**يَبكِي** (yabkī, he cries) from root **ب-ك-ي** (b-k-y, to cry/weep). Defective verb — the final **ي** affects conjugation: present **يَبكِي**, past **بَكَى** (bakā). **بُكَاء** (bukāʾ, crying/weeping — verbal noun), **بَاكٍ** (bākin, one who cries — **فَاعِل** with dropped **ي**).
The sun letter **ط** in **الطِّفل** (aṭ-ṭifl, the child) causes assimilation. **طِفل** has broken plural **أَطفَال** (aṭfāl).

**يَصرُخ** (yaṣrukh, he screams) from root **ص-ر-خ** (ṣ-r-kh, to scream/cry out). **صَرَخَ** (ṣarakha, to scream), **صُرَاخ** (ṣurākh, screaming — verbal noun), **صَرخَة** (ṣarkha, a scream). Sun letter **ص** causes assimilation of ال.
**لَا تَصرُخ** = don't shout — prohibition: **لَا** + present tense (jussive form). The jussive of **يَصرُخ** is the same form here. MSA and colloquial both use this construction for commands.

**يَستَرخِي** (yastarkhi, he relaxes) — Form X of root **ر-خ-و/ي** (r-kh-w, to be loose). Form X = to become/seek a state: **اِسترَخَى** (istarkha, to relax/go loose). Related: **رَخو** (rakhw, loose/soft), **اِرتِخَاء** (irtikhaʾ, relaxation/slackness).
**لَا دَاعِيَ لِـ** (lā dāʿiya li-, there is no need for) — a fixed construction: **دَاعٍ** (dāʿin, reason/motive — **فَاعِل** of root **د-ع-و**, to call/invite).

**غَاضِب** (ghāḍib, angry) — **فَاعِل** active participle from root **غ-ض-ب** (gh-ḍ-b, to be angry). Describes the current state of being angry: **أَنَا غَاضِب** = I am (currently) angry. Feminine: **غَاضِبة** (ghāḍiba).
Contrast: **غَضبَان** (ghaḍbān, furious — **فَعلَان** pattern) implies a stronger, more agitated state. **غَضبَانة** (ghaḍbāna, furious, f.) — this pattern is especially common in colloquial Arabic for emotional states.

**خَائِف** (khāʾif, afraid) — **فَاعِل** active participle from root **خ-و-ف** (kh-w-f, to fear). Describes a current state: **أَنَا خَائِف** = I am afraid. Feminine: **خَائِفة** (khāʾifa).
**كَانَ الطِّفلُ خَائِفاً** — **كَانَ** (kāna) + adjective in the accusative (**خَائِفاً** with tanwin **ـاً**). This is the standard structure for past states: كان + predicate accusative. Note sun letter **ط** in **الطِّفل**: *aṭ-ṭifl*.

**قَلِق** (qaliq, anxious/restless) — **فَعِل** stative adjective from root **ق-ل-ق** (q-l-q, to be restless). Note the doubled root letters (q-l-q) — a reduplicated root. **قَلَق** (qalaq, anxiety — noun), **قَلِقَ** (qaliqa, to be anxious).
Feminine: **قَلِقة** (qaliqa). The preposition **بِشَأنِ** (bi-shaʾni, regarding/about) is very common in MSA: **قَلِق بِشَأنِ** = anxious about. More colloquial: **خَايِف عَلَى** (afraid for).

cards.english: he is nervous / she is nervous (متوتر / متوترة)
cards.grammarNote:
Mood adjectives agree with the person's gender — feminine adds **ة**:
**متوتر / متوترة** (nervous), **غاضب / غاضبة** (angry), **متعب / متعبة** (tired). Match the adjective to who you're describing.

**مُتَوَتِّر** (mutawattir, nervous/tense) — Form V active participle from root **و-ت-ر** (w-t-r, to tighten/string). Form V (**تَفَعَّلَ**): **وَتَّرَ** (wattara, to tighten/make taut) → **تَوَتَّرَ** (tawattara, to become tense). **تَوَتُّر** (tawattur, tension/nervousness — Form V verbal noun).
Feminine: **مُتَوَتِّرة** (mutawattira). Colloquially, Egyptians often say **مُتوَتِّر** or **خَايِف** for nervous.

**مُتَحَمِّس** (mutaḥammis, excited/enthusiastic) — Form V active participle from root **ح-م-س** (ḥ-m-s, to be zealous). Form V: **حَمَّسَ** (ḥammasa, to enthuse someone) → **تَحَمَّسَ** (taḥammasa, to become enthusiastic). **حَمَاس** (ḥamās, enthusiasm/zeal — also the name of the Palestinian movement).
**لِلرِّحلة** (lir-riḥla) = for the trip — **لِـ** (li-, for) + sun letter **ر** causes assimilation: *lir-riḥla*.

**مُبهِج** (mubhij, joyful/delightful) — Form IV active participle from root **ب-ه-ج** (b-h-j, to be radiant). Note the phrase uses **مَرِحة** (mariḥa, cheerful/merry) — **فَعِل** adjective pattern from root **م-ر-ح** (m-r-ḥ, to be jolly). Both describe cheerfulness but differ slightly: **مُبهِج** = causing delight (active), **مَرِح** = being merry (stative).
Feminine agreement: **مَرِحة** agrees with **هي** (she).

**فَخُور** (fakhūr, proud) — **فَعُول** intensive adjective pattern from root **ف-خ-ر** (f-kh-r, to be proud). **فَعُول** describes an enduring quality or strong disposition: **صَبُور** (patient), **شَكُور** (grateful), **غَيُور** (jealous/zealous). **فَخر** (fakhr, pride — noun), **مَفخَرة** (mafkhara, source of pride).
**فَخُور بِكَ** = proud of you — the **بِـ** preposition follows **فَخُور**: be proud of [someone].

**رَاضٍ** (rāḍin, content/satisfied) — **فَاعِل** active participle of root **ر-ض-ي** (r-ḍ-y, to be content/approve). The final **ي** drops before case endings, giving the indefinite form **رَاضٍ** (with tanwin). Definite: **الرَّاضِي** (ar-rāḍī). Feminine: **رَاضِيَة** (rāḍiya).
**رَضِيَ عَن** = to be content with [something]. **رِضَا** (riḍā, satisfaction/approval — also a personal name) from the same root.

**هَادِئ** (hādiʾ, calm/quiet) — **فَاعِل** active participle from root **ه-د-أ** (h-d-ʾ, to be still/calm). Feminine: **هَادِئة** (hādiʾa). **هُدُوء** (hudūʾ, calmness — verbal noun), **تَهدِئة** (tahdiʾa, calming/soothing — Form II verbal noun).
**اِبقَ هَادِئاً** = stay calm — imperative **اِبقَ** (ibqa, stay/remain) from root **ب-ق-ي** (b-q-y) + **هَادِئاً** in accusative as a state complement (ḥāl). This structure means 'remain in the state of being calm.'

**مَضغُوط** (maḍghūṭ, stressed/under pressure) — passive participle **مَفعُول** from root **ض-غ-ط** (ḍ-gh-ṭ, to press/squeeze). Literally 'pressed upon/squeezed.' **ضَغط** (ḍaghṭ, pressure), **ضَغط الدَّم** (blood pressure), **ضَغط العَمَل** (work pressure).
In MSA, **مُجهَد** (mujhad, exhausted) or **تَحتَ ضَغط** (under pressure) are also used. **مَضغُوط** is especially common in Levantine and Gulf colloquial Arabic for 'stressed out.'

**مَغلُوب عَلَى أَمرِهِ** (maghūb ʿalā amrihi) = overwhelmed, literally 'overcome in his matter.' **مَغلُوب** (maghūb, overcome — passive participle of root **غ-ل-ب**, to overcome/defeat). **أَمر** (amr, matter/affair/command). The possessive suffix **ـهِ** refers to the subject.
**بِسَبَب** (bi-sabab, because of/due to) — preposition + noun: **سَبَب** (sabab, reason/cause) from root **س-ب-ب** (s-b-b). Plural: **أَسبَاب** (asbāb, reasons).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel overwhelmed by the work.
cards.phrase: أشعر أنني مغلوب على أمري بسبب العمل.
cards.phraseRomanized: ash'ur annani maghlub 'ala amri bi-sabab al-'amal.

cards.grammarNote:
**نَشِيط** (nashīṭ, energetic/active) — **فَعِيل** adjective pattern from root **ن-ش-ط** (n-sh-ṭ, to be active/vigorous). **نَشَاط** (nashāṭ, activity/energy — verbal noun), **أَنشِطة** (anshiṭa, activities — broken plural **أَفعِلة**).
Feminine agreement: **نَشِيطَة** (nashīṭa) agrees with **هي** (she). The predicate adjective takes no definite article: **هي نَشِيطَة** = she is energetic (equational sentence, no verb 'to be').

**جداً** (jiddan) = very — and it comes **after** the adjective, not before:
**متعب جداً** (very tired), **سعيد جداً** (very happy), **جميل جداً** (very beautiful).

**مُتعَب** (mutʿab, tired) — passive participle **مُفعَل** from root **ت-ع-ب** (t-ʿ-b, to be tired). **أَتعَبَ** (atʿaba, to tire someone out — Form IV), **مُتعَب** = 'made tired/worn out.' **تَعَب** (taʿab, tiredness — noun), **تَعبَان** (taʿbān, tired — colloquial **فَعلَان** pattern, very common in spoken Arabic).
In MSA prefer **مُتعَب**; colloquially **تَعبَان** is more natural: أنا تعبان = I'm tired.

**مُنهَك** (munhak, exhausted) — passive participle from root **ن-ه-ك** (n-h-k, to exhaust/wear down). **أَنهَكَ** (anhaka, to exhaust — Form IV), **نُهُوك** (nuhūk, exhaustion — verbal noun). The **مُفعَل** pattern = 'made to be' in the root state: **مُنهَك** = 'made completely worn down.'
Distinguish degrees: **مُتعَب** (tired) < **مُنهَك** (exhausted) < **مُنهَك تَمَاماً** (completely drained).

**فُضُولِيّ** (fuḍūlī, curious/nosy) — nisba adjective from **فُضُول** (fuḍūl, curiosity/nosiness). Root **ف-ض-ل** (f-ḍ-l, excess/virtue): **فُضُول** originally meant 'excess matters / things beyond one's need,' hence nosiness or curiosity. **فَضِيلة** (faḍīla, virtue — same root), **أَفضَل** (afḍal, better/best).
Note: **فُضُولِيّ** can mean 'nosy' (peeking into others' affairs) as well as 'curious' — context determines the tone. A more neutral word is **مُتَفَضِّل** or **فَضُولِيّ بِطَبعِهِ** (naturally curious).

Body parts take the same **possessive suffixes** as other nouns:
**يدي** (my hand), **يدك** (your hand), **رأسه** (his head), **عينها** (her eye). The **ـي** ending = 'my'.

A common way to say something hurts: the body part (+ 'my') as subject + **يؤلمني** ('it pains me'):
**رأسي يؤلمني** (my head hurts), **بطني يؤلمني** (my stomach hurts). The verb agrees in gender: **يدي تؤلمني** (fem.).

The adjective comes **after** the body part and agrees with it. Non-human plurals take a **feminine singular** adjective:
**عيون كبيرة** (big eyes), **يد قوية** (a strong hand), **شعر طويل** (long hair).

To express pain: **[body part] يؤلمني** (yu'limuni) = '[body part] hurts me' (masculine nouns) / **تؤلمني** (tu'limuni) (feminine nouns).
Alternatively: **عندي ألم في** [body part] (indi alam fi...) = I have pain in [body part].

**شَعر** (shaʿr, hair) is a collective noun — it refers to hair as a mass. For a single strand: **شَعرَة** (shaʿra). Root **ش-ع-ر** (sh-ʿ-r, to feel/be aware/have hair). Same root as **شِعر** (shiʿr, poetry) and **شَاعِر** (shāʿir, poet) — the overlap of sensitivity and hair.
**لَدَيهَا** (ladayhā) = she has — possessive preposition **لَدَى** + feminine suffix **ـهَا** (hā, her). **شَعر طَوِيل** — indefinite noun + adjective, no article.

**وَجه** (wajh, face) from root **و-ج-ه** (w-j-h, to face/direct). **وَجَّهَ** (wajjaha, to direct — Form II), **اِتَّجَهَ** (ittajaha, to head toward — Form VIII), **وِجهَة** (wijha, direction/viewpoint), **وُجِهَ إِليهِ** (to be directed at).
Possessive: **وَجهُكَ** (wajhuka, your face m.) — suffix **ـكَ** (-ka). Imperative **اِغسِل** (ighsil, wash!) from root **غ-س-ل** (gh-s-l, to wash) — Form I imperative.

**عَين** (ʿayn, eye) is feminine. Dual: **عَينَان** (ʿaynān, two eyes). The phrase **عَينَاهُ زَرقَاوَان** uses the dual subject + dual adjective. **زَرقَاء** (zarqāʾ, blue, feminine) → dual **زَرقَاوَان** (zarqāwān).
Note: **عَين** also means 'spring of water' and 'essence/self' — a beautifully polysemous root. The letter **ع** itself is named *ʿayn* because it was associated with the shape of an eye in ancient Semitic scripts.

**أُذن** (udhn, ear) is feminine. Dual: **أُذُنَان** (udhunan, two ears). The verb **تُؤلِمُني** uses the feminine form **تُـ** because the ear is feminine — **يُؤلِمُني** would be used for masculine body parts.
Root **أ-ذ-ن** (ʾ-dh-n, to permit/give ear): **أَذِنَ** (adhina, to allow), **أَذَان** (adhān, call to prayer — the announcement one 'gives ear' to). **مَأذُون** (maʾdhūn, authorized person).

**أَنف** (anf, nose) is masculine. Root **أ-ن-ف** (ʾ-n-f, nose/pride/reluctance). **أَنِفَ** (anifa, to disdain — literally 'to be nose-proud'), **أَنَفَة** (anafa, pride/disdain). The same root gives us pride idioms: **شَامِخ الأَنف** (nose held high = arrogant).
The adjective **بَارِد** (bārid, cold) is masculine and agrees with **أَنف** (masculine). Compare: **رَقبَتِي بَارِدَة** (my neck is cold) — feminine **ة** because neck is feminine.

**فَم** (fam, mouth) — an unusual word: it is one of the few Arabic nouns with no clear trilateral root. In possessive constructions the **م** changes: **فَمِي** (famī, my mouth), **فَمُكَ** (famuka, your mouth), but **فُو** (fū) in construct: **فُو الإِنسَان** (fū al-insān, the human mouth) — a classical form.
**اِفتَح** (iftaḥ, open! — imperative Form I) from root **ف-ت-ح** (f-t-ḥ, to open). **فَتح** also means 'conquest/opening' — Saladin's conquest of Jerusalem was called **الفَتح**.

**شَفة** (shafa, lip) — tā marbūṭa **ة** signals a feminine noun. Dual: **شَفَتَان** (shafatān, two lips). In the phrase, **شَفَتَاهَا** = her two lips (dual possessive). The color adjective **حَمرَاء** (ḥamrāʾ, red, feminine) → dual **حَمرَاوَان** (ḥamrāwān).
Note: tā marbūṭa (**ة**) appears at the end of many feminine nouns and adjectives. It is pronounced **ة** (a) in pause but **ت** (t) when followed by another word.

**سِنّ** (sinn, tooth) is feminine. Dual: **سِنَّان** (sinnān, two teeth). Broken plural: **أَسنَان** (asnān, teeth — pattern **أَفعَال**). Root **س-ن-ن** (s-n-n, to sharpen/set). **سِنّ** also means 'age/year': **كَم سِنُّهُ؟** = how old is he?
The verb **تُؤلِمُني** is feminine to agree with **سِنّ** (feminine). The phrase **أَسنَان** (teeth, plural) is used in dental contexts: **طَبِيب الأَسنَان** (dentist — literally 'doctor of teeth').

**لِسَان** (lisān, tongue/language) is masculine. Root **ل-س-ن** (l-s-n, tongue/language). The word covers both the physical tongue and 'language/tongue' in a linguistic sense: **اللِّسَان العَرَبِيّ** = the Arabic tongue/language. Plural: **أَلسِنة** (alsina, tongues — broken plural **أَفعِلة**).
**أَخرِج** (akhrij, take out! — imperative Form IV) from root **خ-ر-ج** (kh-r-j, to exit). Form IV imperative = causative command: 'cause to come out.'

**رَقَبة** (raqaba, neck) — tā marbūṭa **ة** marks it as feminine. Root **ر-ق-ب** (r-q-b, to watch/guard). **رَقِيب** (raqīb, watchman/guard — **فَعِيل**), **مُرَاقَبة** (murāqaba, surveillance/observation — Form III verbal noun). The neck was linked to watching/looking out.
**مُتَصَلِّبة** (mutaṣalliba, stiff, feminine) — Form V active participle from root **ص-ل-ب** (ṣ-l-b, to be hard/rigid). Feminine agrees with **رَقَبة** (feminine).

**ذِرَاع** (dhirāʿ, arm/forearm) is both masculine and feminine — classical Arabic allows both genders. Dual: **ذِرَاعَان** (dhirāʿān, two arms). Root **ذ-ر-ع** (dh-r-ʿ, forearm/measure). **ذِرَاع** was also a unit of length (cubit = forearm length).
**كَسَرتُ** (kasartu, I broke) from root **ك-س-ر** (k-s-r, to break). Past tense first-person singular ends in **ـتُ** (-tu): **ذَهَبتُ** (I went), **أَكَلتُ** (I ate).

Arabic has a special **dual** for exactly two — add **ـان** (or **ـين**): ideal for paired body parts:
**يد → يدان** (two hands), **عين → عينان** (two eyes), **رِجل → رِجلان** (two legs). No number word needed.

Arabic has a dual form for pairs: **يد** (yad = hand) → **يدان** (yadan = two hands).
In **اغسل يديك** (ighsil yadayk), **يديك** is the dual possessive.
Dual forms apply across paired body parts: **عينان** (two eyes), **رجلان** (two legs).

**إِصبَع** (iṣbaʿ, finger/toe) can be masculine or feminine. Broken plural: **أَصَابِع** (aṣābiʿ — pattern **أَفَاعِل**). Root **ص-ب-ع** (ṣ-b-ʿ, finger). **إِصبَع القَدَم** = toe (literally 'finger of the foot').
**قَطَعَ** (qaṭaʿa, to cut) from root **ق-ط-ع** (q-ṭ-ʿ, to cut/sever). A productive root: **قَطِيعة** (qaṭīʿa, estrangement), **اِنقِطَاع** (inqiṭāʿ, interruption — Form VII verbal noun).

**صَدر** (ṣadr, chest/breast) is masculine. Root **ص-د-ر** (ṣ-d-r, to issue from/chest). **صَدَرَ** (ṣadara, to issue/be issued), **صُدُور** (ṣudūr, chests — broken plural **فُعُول**), **مَصدَر** (maṣdar, source/verbal noun — the 'issuing point' of action).
**عِندَهُ** (ʿindahu, he has — literally 'at him') + **أَلَم** (ʾalam, pain): **عِندَهُ أَلَم فِي الصَّدر** = he has pain in the chest. **الصَّدر** — sun letter **ص** causes assimilation.

**ظَهر** (ẓahr, back) is masculine. Root **ظ-ه-ر** (ẓ-h-r, to appear/back). **ظَهَرَ** (ẓahara, to appear/become visible), **ظَاهِرة** (ẓāhira, phenomenon — 'something that appears'), **ظُهُور** (ẓuhūr, appearance/back — verbal noun). The verb **يُؤلِمُني** is masculine (**يُـ** prefix) to agree with **ظَهر** (masculine).
**أَسفَل الظَّهر** (asfal aẓ-ẓahr, lower back) — **أَسفَل** (asfal, lower/bottom) + definite **الظَّهر** in an iḍāfa chain. Sun letter **ظ**: *aẓ-ẓahr*.

**كَتِف** (katif, shoulder) can be masculine or feminine — both genders are used in classical Arabic. Root **ك-ت-ف** (k-t-f, shoulder/to bind the arms). Dual: **كَتِفَان** (katifān). Broken plural: **أَكتَاف** (aktāf — pattern **أَفعَال**).
**يُؤلِمُني** (yuʾlimunī, hurts me) — masculine verb form agreeing with **كَتِف** when treated as masculine. The suffix **ـنِي** (-nī) = me (object pronoun attached to verb).

**مِرفَق** (mirfaq, elbow) — **مِفعَل** instrument/place pattern from root **ر-ف-ق** (r-f-q, to accompany/be gentle). Literally 'the place of companionship' (the elbow bends toward the body, or the arm bends to accompany a companion). **رِفق** (rifq, gentleness), **رَفِيق** (rafīq, companion/comrade — **فَعِيل**), **مُرَافِق** (murāfiq, escort/accompanying).
Broken plural: **مَرَافِق** (marāfiq — **مَفَاعِل**). Masculine noun: verb **يُؤلِمُنِي** agrees.

**رُكبَة** (rukba, knee) — tā marbūṭa **ة** marks it as feminine. Dual: **رُكبَتَان** (rukbatān, two knees). Root **ر-ك-ب** (r-k-b, to ride/kneel). **رَكَبَ** (rakaba, to kneel/ride), **رَاكِب** (rākib, rider — **فَاعِل**), **مَركَبة** (markaba, vehicle — **مَفعَلة** pattern).
**أَصَبتُ فِي** (aṣabtu fī, I hurt/injured in) from root **ص-و-ب** (ṣ-w-b, to hit/be correct): **أَصَابَ** (aṣāba, to hit/injure — Form IV). Past tense 1st person: **أَصَبتُ**.

**سَاق** (sāq, leg/shin) is feminine. Dual: **سَاقَان** (sāqān, two legs). Root **س-و-ق** (s-w-q, to drive/leg). **سَوَّقَ** (sawwaqa, to market — Form II), **سُوق** (sūq, market — 'the place one drives/goes to'). All from the same root!
**مُتعَبة** (mutʿaba, tired, feminine) agrees with **سَاق** (feminine). The predicate adjective must match the noun: feminine noun → feminine adjective.

**قَدَم** (qadam, foot) is feminine. Dual: **قَدَمَان** (qadamān). Possessive dual: **قَدَمَايَ** (qadamāya, my two feet). Root **ق-د-م** (q-d-m, foot/to come forward): **قَدِيم** (qadīm, old/ancient), **مُقَدِّمة** (muqaddima, introduction — 'what comes first'), **قَدَّمَ** (qaddama, to present — Form II).
**تُؤلِمَانِّي** — dual feminine verb (prefix **تُـ** + dual suffix **ـَان**) + object suffix **ـِّي** (me). This is the dual verb form matching dual subject **قَدَمَاي**.

**إِصبَع القَدَم** (iṣbaʿ al-qadam) = toe, literally 'finger of the foot' — an iḍāfa chain. Arabic uses the same word for finger and toe, distinguished only by adding **القَدَم** (the foot). Plural: **أَصَابِع القَدَم** (aṣābiʿ al-qadam, toes).
**اِصطَدَمَ بِـ** (iṣṭadama bi-, to collide with/stub against — Form VIII): root **ص-د-م** (ṣ-d-m, to crash/collide). Form VIII inserts **ت** after the first radical: **ص** + **ط** (assimilation of ت after ص) → **اِصطَدَمَ**.

**بَطن** (baṭn, stomach/belly) is masculine. Root **ب-ط-ن** (b-ṭ-n, inside/belly). **بَاطِن** (bāṭin, inner/hidden — **فَاعِل**), **بَاطِنِيَّة** (bāṭiniyya, internal medicine), **بُطُون** (buṭūn, bellies — broken plural **فُعُول**). The inner/hidden sense of the root extends to: **عِلم البَاطِن** = esoteric knowledge.
Verb **يُؤلِمُني** is masculine (prefix **يُـ**) agreeing with **بَطن** (masculine).

**جِسم** (jism, body) is masculine. Root **ج-س-م** (j-s-m, body/to be corporeal). **جَسَد** (jasad, body — especially with spiritual connotation), **مُجَسَّم** (mujassam, three-dimensional/embodied — Form II passive participle). Arabic has two body words: **جِسم** (physical body as a whole) and **جَسَد** (body esp. as vessel of the soul).
**البَشَرِيّ** (al-basharī, human — nisba adjective) from **بَشَر** (bashar, human/mankind): **بَشَر** is the collective noun for humanity.

**قَلب** (qalb, heart) is masculine. Root **ق-ل-ب** (q-l-b, to turn/flip). **قَلَبَ** (qalaba, to flip/overturn), **اِنقَلَبَ** (inqalaba, to be overturned/revolution — Form VII), **تَقَلُّب** (taqallub, fluctuation/turning). The heart was called **قَلب** because it 'turns over' (beats/changes states).
**يَدُقُّ** (yaduqqu, it beats) from root **د-ق-ق** (d-q-q, to beat/knock/be precise). **دَقَّة** (daqqa, a beat/knock), **دَقِيق** (daqīq, precise/minute — also flour!).

**عَضَلة** (ʿaḍala, muscle) — tā marbūṭa **ة** marks it as feminine. Root **ع-ض-ل** (ʿ-ḍ-l, muscle/difficulty). **عَضَّلَ** (ʿaḍḍala, to make difficult — Form II), **مُعضِلة** (muʿḍila, dilemma/difficult problem — literally 'a muscular/knotty thing'). Plural: **عَضَلَات** (ʿaḍalāt, muscles — sound feminine plural).
**شَدَدتُ** (shadadtu, I pulled) from root **ش-د-د** (sh-d-d, to pull/tighten). Geminated root: **شَدَّ** → past 1st person **شَدَدتُ**.

**جِلد** (jild, skin/hide/leather) is masculine. Root **ج-ل-د** (j-l-d, skin/to flog). **جِلدِيَّة** (jildiyya, dermatology — nisba adjective), **جِلدِيّ** (jildī, dermatological), **مُجَلَّد** (mujallad, bound book — 'covered in skin/leather').
**نَاعِم** (nāʿim, soft/smooth — **فَاعِل** pattern) from root **ن-ع-م** (n-ʿ-m, to be soft/pleasant). **نِعمَة** (niʿma, blessing/grace) and **نَعَم** (naʿam, yes/domestic animals) share this root.

**دَم** (dam, blood) is masculine. Root **د-م-و/ي** (d-m-w, blood). **دَمَوِيّ** (damawī, bloody/blood-related), **ضَغط الدَّم** (blood pressure). Note: **دَم** is a defective noun — its full form would be **دَمَو** or **دَمَي**, but only the base form **دَم** is used.
**تَبَرَّعَ بِـ** (tabarraʿa bi-, to donate — Form V): **بَرَّعَ** (barraʿa, to give generously) → **تَبَرَّعَ** (tabarraʿa, to donate/volunteer). **تَبَرُّع** (tabarruʿ, donation). The **بِـ** preposition introduces what is donated.

**دِمَاغ** (dimāgh, brain) is masculine. MSA also uses **مُخّ** (mukhkh, brain/marrow) from root **م-خ-خ** (m-kh-kh). **دِمَاغ** from root **د-م-غ** (d-m-gh, brain/to crush). **دَمَغَ** (damagha, to crush/stamp), **دَامِغ** (dāmigh, crushing/decisive — **فَاعِل**).
**مُعَقَّد** (muʿaqqad, complex/complicated) — Form II passive participle from root **ع-ق-د** (ʿ-q-d, to knot/contract). Literally 'knotted.' **عَقد** (ʿaqd, knot/contract), **مَعقُود** (contracted).

**صَدر** (ṣadr) serves as both 'chest' (general) and 'breast' — context distinguishes. The word is masculine despite often referring to female anatomy. Root **ص-د-ر** (ṣ-d-r, to issue/chest). **شَعَرَت** (shaʿarat) — past feminine: root **ش-ع-ر** + feminine suffix **ـت** (-at).
**بِأَلَمٍ** (bi-alamin, with/of pain) — the **بِـ** preposition after **شَعَرَ** is obligatory. **صَدرِهَا** = her chest — possessive suffix **ـهَا** (hā, her/its).
cards.englishPhrase: She felt pain in her chest.

cards.grammarNote:
**يَرَى** (yarā, he sees) — defective verb from root **ر-أ-ي** (r-ʾ-y, to see/think). The hamza drops in many forms: present **يَرَى**, past **رَأَى** (raʾā). **رُؤيَة** (ruʾya, sight/vision — verbal noun), **رَأي** (raʾy, opinion — 'what one sees').
**أَستَطِيع** (astaṭīʿ, I can/am able) — Form X of root **ط-و-ع** (ṭ-w-ʿ, to obey/be capable). Form X = to seek the ability. **بِوُضُوح** (bi-wuḍūḥ, clearly) — root **و-ض-ح** (w-ḍ-ḥ, to be clear).

**يَسمَع** (yasmaʿ, he hears) from root **س-م-ع** (s-m-ʿ, to hear). **سَمِعَ** (samiʿa, to hear — Form I), **سَمَاع** (samāʿ, hearing/listening to music), **اِستَمَعَ** (istamaʿa, to listen attentively — Form X). Distinguish: **سَمِعَ** = passive hearing; **اِستَمَعَ** = active listening.
**لَا أَسمَعُكَ** — **لَا** + present tense = present negation: 'I don't/can't hear you.' The suffix **ـكَ** (ka) = you (masculine). For a woman: **لَا أَسمَعُكِ** (-ki).

**يَشُمّ** (yashumm, he smells) from root **ش-م-م** (sh-m-m, to smell). A geminate root: the last two radicals are the same (**م-م**). Present: **يَشُمّ** (yashumm), past: **شَمَّ** (shamma). **رَائِحة** (rāʾiḥa, smell/scent — **فَاعِلة** feminine active participle) from root **ر-و-ح** (r-w-ḥ, breath/rest).
**الزُّهُور** (az-zuhūr, flowers) — broken plural of **زَهرَة** (zahra, flower) — pattern **فُعُول**. Sun letter **ز** causes assimilation: *az-zuhūr*.

**يَتَذَوَّق** (yatadhawwaq, he tastes) — Form V of root **ذ-و-ق** (dh-w-q, to taste). Form V (**تَفَعَّلَ**): **ذَاقَ** (dhāqa, to taste briefly) → **تَذَوَّقَ** (tadhawwaqa, to taste carefully/appreciate). **ذَوق** (dhawq, taste/aesthetic sense), **ذَوَّاق** (dhawwāq, one with refined taste — **فَعَّال** intensive).
**الحِسَاء** (al-ḥisāʾ, soup/broth) from root **ح-س-و** (ḥ-s-w, to sip). The imperative **تَذَوَّق** drops the initial **تَـ** prefix: Form V imperative.

**يَلمَس** (yalmas, he touches) from root **ل-م-س** (l-m-s, to touch). **لَمسَة** (lamsa, a touch/stroke), **مَلمَس** (malmas, texture/feel — **مَفعَل** place/instrument noun), **لَامَسَ** (lāmasa, to touch/be in contact with — Form III).
**لَا تَلمَس** = don't touch — prohibition: **لَا** + jussive present tense. **ذلِك** (dhālika, that) is the demonstrative for distant/removed objects. Nearby: **هَذَا** (hādhā, this).

**يَتَنَفَّس** (yatanaffas, he breathes) — Form V of root **ن-ف-س** (n-f-s, breath/soul). Form V implies a continuous/repeated action: **نَفَّسَ** (naffasa, to relieve) → **تَنَفَّسَ** (tanaffasa, to breathe steadily). **تَنَفُّس** (tanaffus, breathing — verbal noun).
**بِبُطء** (bi-buṭʾ, slowly) — **بِـ** + **بُطء** (buṭʾ, slowness) from root **ب-ط-أ** (b-ṭ-ʾ, to be slow). This **بِـ + noun** pattern creates adverbial phrases: **بِسُرعَة** (quickly), **بِهُدُوء** (calmly).

**يَنحَنِي** (yanḥanī, he bends) — Form VII of root **ح-ن-و/ي** (ḥ-n-w, to bend/curve). Form VII (**اِنفَعَلَ**) is reflexive/passive: **حَنَا** (ḥanā, to bend something) → **اِنحَنَى** (inḥanā, to bend oneself/bow). **حَنِين** (ḥanīn, longing/yearning — literally 'a bending of the soul toward something').
**رُكبَتَيكَ** (rukbatayka, your two knees) — dual possessive: **رُكبَتَان** (dual) → **رُكبَتَي** (construct) + **ـكَ** (your).

**يَمُدّ** (yamudd, he stretches/extends) from root **م-د-د** (m-d-d, to extend). Geminate root: **مَدَّ** (madda, to stretch). **مَدَّة** (madda, a stretch/duration), **إِمدَاد** (imdād, supply/reinforcement — Form IV verbal noun), **مَدِينة** (madīna, city — literally 'the extended place').
**ذِرَاعَيكَ** (dhirāʿayka, your two arms) — dual possessive. Imperative **مُدَّ** = stretch! — geminate verb: the doubled **د** is written with shadda: مُدَّ.

**يَتَعَرَّق** (yataʿarraq, he sweats) — Form V of root **ع-ر-ق** (ʿ-r-q, sweat/vein). Form V = to undergo the process: **عَرِقَ** (ʿariqa, to sweat — Form I stative) or **تَعَرَّقَ** (taʿarraqa, to perspire). **عَرَق** (ʿaraq, sweat — noun; also the anise liquor), **عِرق** (ʿirq, vein/nerve/root — same root!).
**عِندَمَا** (ʿindamā, when — subordinating conjunction) = at the time that.

**يَشعُر** (yashʿur, he feels) from root **ش-ع-ر** (sh-ʿ-r, to feel/perceive). Always used with **بِـ** when feeling an emotion: **شَعَرَ بِـ** = to feel [noun]. In medical contexts, **كيفَ تَشعُر؟** = how do you feel? Note: physical sensation often uses **يُؤلِمُني** (hurts me) or **عِندِي** (I have [symptom]) instead.
**كَيفَ** (kayfa, how) introduces the question. No verb 'to be' is needed in the question.

**يُفَكِّر** (yufakkir, he thinks) — Form II of root **ف-ك-ر** (f-k-r, to think). Form II intensifies: **فَكَرَ** (fakara, to think once) → **فَكَّرَ** (fakkara, to think carefully/reflect). **فِكر** (fikr, thought), **فِكرَة** (fikra, idea), **تَفكِير** (tafkīr, thinking — Form II verbal noun).
**بِمَ** (bi-mā) = about what? — **بِـ** (about) + **مَا** (what). The **ما** loses its final **ا** before another word in classical style. **تُفَكِّر فِي** or **تُفَكِّر بِـ** = to think about.

**يَتَحَرَّك** (yataḥarrak, he moves) — Form V of root **ح-ر-ك** (ḥ-r-k, to move). Form V is reflexive: **حَرَّكَ** (ḥarraka, to move something — Form II) → **تَحَرَّكَ** (taḥarraka, to move oneself). **تَحرِيك** (taḥrīk, moving something — Form II verbal noun), **حَرَكَة** (ḥaraka, movement/vowel mark in Arabic script).
**لَا أَستَطِيع + verbal noun** = I can't [do action]. **تَحرِيك** is the verbal noun used as direct object here.

**نَاعِم** (nāʿim, soft/smooth) — **فَاعِل** active participle from root **ن-ع-م** (n-ʿ-m, to be gentle/soft). Feminine: **نَاعِمة** (nāʿima). Related words: **نِعمَة** (niʿma, blessing), **نَعَم** (naʿam, yes — agreement/acceptance), **أَنعَم** (anʿama, to bestow blessings — Form IV).
**النَّسِيج** (an-nasīj, the tissue/fabric) — sun letter **ن** causes assimilation. **نَسَجَ** (nasaja, to weave), **نَسِيج** (nasīj, fabric/tissue — **فَعِيل**) from root **ن-س-ج**.

**مُؤلِم** (muʾlim, painful/sore) — Form IV active participle from root **أ-ل-م** (ʾ-l-m, to hurt). **أَلَمَ** → **أَلَّمَ** / **أَوجَعَ** = to cause pain. Feminine: **مُؤلِمة** (muʾlima).
**عَضَلَاتِي مُؤلِمَة** — non-human plurals (here **عَضَلَات**, muscles) take a **feminine singular** predicate adjective in classical Arabic: **مُؤلِمَة** (not **مُؤلِمُون**). This is the famous rule: 'broken and sound feminine plurals of non-humans are treated as feminine singular.'

**أَيسَر** (aysar, left — masculine superlative-form adjective) from root **ي-س-ر** (y-s-r, to be easy/left). **يُسرَى** (yusr ā, left, feminine) / **أَيسَر** (aysar, left, masculine). Ironically the root **ي-س-ر** means 'easy' — the left hand was the 'easier' in ancient usage.
Feminine form **اليُسرَى** (al-yusr ā) is used here because **رُكبَة** (knee) is feminine. Compare: **اليَمِين** / **اليُمنَى** (right, masculine/feminine) from root **ي-م-ن** (y-m-n, right/blessing).

**أَيمَن** (aymayn, right — masculine) / **اليُمنَى** (al-yumnā, the right, feminine) from root **ي-م-ن** (y-m-n, right/blessing/south). **يَمِين** (yamīn, right side/oath), **يُمنَى** (yumnā, right — feminine form), **يَمَن** (Yaman, Yemen — the land to the right when facing Mecca from Arabia).
The phrase uses **اليُمنَى** (feminine) because **ذِرَاع** (arm) is feminine. The adjective follows the noun and takes the definite article to match: **ذِرَاعِي اليُمنَى** = my right arm.

**عُلوِيّ** (ʿulwī, upper/elevated) — nisba adjective from **عُلوّ** (ʿuluww, height/elevation) from root **ع-ل-و** (ʿ-l-w, to be high). **عَالٍ** (ʿālin, high — **فَاعِل**), **أَعلَى** (aʿlā, higher/highest), **عَلِيّ** (ʿAlī, the name meaning 'exalted').
**الجُزء** (al-juzʾ, the part) from root **ج-ز-أ** (j-z-ʾ, to divide). **جُزء** = part/portion; plural **أَجزَاء** (ajzāʾ — pattern **أَفعَال**).

**سُفلِيّ** (suflī, lower) — nisba adjective from **سُفل** (sufl, bottom/below) from root **س-ف-ل** (s-f-l, to be low). **أَسفَل** (asfal, lower/bottom — elative **أَفعَل** pattern), **سُفلِيَّات** (sufliyyāt, lower things).
**أَسفَل الظَّهر** (asfal aẓ-ẓahr) = the lower back — iḍāfa: **أَسفَل** (the lower part) + **الظَّهر** (the back). Sun letter **ظ** in **الظَّهر**: *aẓ-ẓahr*. Note **عِندَهُ أَلَم** = he has pain (possession construction).

packs.name: Equational Sentences — No Verb To Be

cards.grammarNote: Arabic drops the present-tense verb 'to be.' Simply place the subject next to the predicate. القهوة (the coffee) + ساخنة (hot, fem.) = 'The coffee is hot.' No linking verb needed.
أنا (I) + جائع (hungry, masc.) — the pronoun fills the 'subject' slot and the adjective fills the 'predicate' slot. Female speaker: أنا جائعة (ana ja'ia).

cards.english: My sister is a student at the university.
The weather was beautiful. (past tense — kana appears)
cards.grammarNote: Past tense 'to be' = كان (kana). Only present tense drops the verb. كان (kana) = was/were; كانت (kanat) = was (fem.); سيكون (sayakun) = will be (future).

cards.english: the happy man (noun phrase) vs. The man is happy. (sentence)
cards.grammarNote: Key distinction: الرجل السعيد (the happy man) = both definite, modifier. الرجل سعيد (The man is happy) = predicate adjective stays INDEFINITE. This definiteness difference is how you tell noun phrases from equational sentences.
Arabic drops 'to be' in the present. أنا (I) + سعيد (happy, masc.) = 'I am happy.' Female speaker: أنا سعيدة (ana sa'ida).
سعداء is the broken plural of سعيد. Arabic has two types of plural: sound (add ون/ات) and broken (internal vowel change).

cards.english: Count from zero to five in Arabic.
cards.word: صفر، واحد، اثنان، ثلاثة، أربعة، خمسة
cards.romanized: sifr, wāḥid, ithnān, thalātha, arbaʿa, khamsa.
cards.grammarNote: These are the cardinal numbers. 1 and 2 agree in gender with the noun they count. 3–10 use the opposite gender — that rule starts with ثلاثة/ثلاث.

cards.english: Count from six to ten in Arabic.
What is the gender reversal rule for Arabic numbers 3–10?
cards.word: Numbers 3–10 use the OPPOSITE gender of the noun they count.
cards.grammarNote: Masculine noun → feminine number (with ة). Feminine noun → masculine number (without ة). Example: ثلاثة كتب (three books, masc. noun → fem. number) vs. ثلاث بنات (three girls, fem. noun → masc. number).
كتاب (kitāb = book) is masculine, so the number takes the feminine form ثلاثة (with ة). The counted noun appears in the plural: كتب (kutub).
بنت (bint = girl) is feminine, so the number takes the masculine form ثلاث (without ة). The counted noun is plural: بنات (banāt).
أصدقاء (aṣdiqāʾ = friends) is masculine plural, so the number is feminine: خمسة (khamsa, with ة).
Compound numbers above 20 put the unit first: واحد وعشرون = 'one and twenty' = 21. The و (wa = and) connects them.
مئة (miʾa) = 100. ألف (alf) = 1000. To say 200: مئتان (miʾatān, dual form). To say 2000: ألفان (alfān).
Time uses ordinal numbers: الثانية (the second), الثالثة (the third), etc. الساعة (al-sāʿa) = the clock/hour. No verb needed — this is an equational sentence.
النصف (al-niṣf) = the half. الربع (al-rubʿ) = the quarter. So: الثالثة والربع = 3:15 (three and a quarter).
تذاكر (tadhākir = tickets) is feminine, so the number is masculine: ثلاث (thalāth, without ة).
اليوم (al-yawm) = today. Can open or close the sentence: اليوم أنا مشغول (Today I am busy) or أنا مشغول اليوم (I am busy today). Both are natural.
الآن (al-ān) = now (formal and colloquial). بعدين (baʿdain) = later, very common in colloquial Arabic. The formal equivalent is لاحقاً (lāḥiqan).
قبل (qabl) and بعد (baʿd) can stand alone as adverbs or precede a noun: قبل الغداء (qabl al-ghadāʾ = before lunch), بعد العمل (baʿd al-ʿamal = after work).

cards.english: What day does the Arabic week start on?
cards.grammarNote: The Arabic week runs Sunday (الأحد) through Saturday (السبت). Friday (الجمعة) is the day of communal prayer and is the primary day off in many Arab countries.
الجمعة comes from جمع (jam = gathering/congregation). Friday is the most culturally significant weekday — صلاة الجمعة (ṣalāt al-jumʿa) is the obligatory Friday noon prayer.
To say 'on [day],' use يوم (yawm = day of) before the day name, or simply use the day name with the definite article: الاثنين = on Monday.
أبداً (abadan = never) must be paired with a negated verb: لا أذهب أبداً (lā adhhab abadan = I never go). Alone in response to a question, أبداً means 'absolutely not.'

cards.english: I always drink coffee in the morning.
كِتَاب means ___ and comes from root ___
cards.grammarNote: كِتَاب (kitāb) follows the CiCāC pattern — a common shape for abstract or object nouns. The three consonants ك، ت، ب are the skeleton; the vowels i and ā give it its noun shape.

cards.english: What does the pattern CāCiC (فَاعِل) mean?
cards.word: Active participle — the doer of the action. e.g., كَاتِب (kātib) = writer, عَامِل (ʿāmil) = worker, دَارِس (dāris) = student/studier
cards.grammarNote: The CāCiC pattern is one of the most productive in Arabic. Spot it by the long ā vowel after the first root consonant and a kasra (i) under the second. It always means 'the one who does X.'

cards.word: Root د-ر-س (d-r-s) = studying/learning. مَدْرَسَة (madrasa) = school — a place of studying.
cards.grammarNote: مَدْرَسَة follows the maCCaCa pattern — a place-noun template. The م prefix + root + short a vowels = 'the place where this root's action happens.' Same pattern as مَكْتَبَة (maktaba, library/bookstore).

cards.word: مَكْتُوب (maktūb) = written / a letter — something that has been written.
cards.grammarNote: The maCCūC (مَفْعُول) pattern is the passive participle across virtually all roots. The long ū vowel on the third consonant is the key marker. Compare: مَكْتَب (maktab, office — place noun, short a) vs. مَكْتُوب (maktūb, written — passive, long ū).

cards.english: What root do كَتَبَ، كِتَاب، كَاتِب، and مَكْتَبَة all share?
cards.word: Root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b) = writing. All four words contain the consonants ك، ت، ب in that order.
cards.grammarNote: To find the root, strip away the vowels and any م prefix. What consonants remain, in order? That is your root. كِتَاب → ك ت ب. مَكْتَبَة → (drop م) → ك ت ب.

cards.english: What role does the maCCaC / maCCaCa pattern play?
cards.word: Place of action noun. مَكْتَب (maktab) = office/desk, مَدْرَسَة (madrasa) = school, مَعْمَل (maʿmal) = laboratory.
cards.grammarNote: Any word starting with م followed by a root's consonants with short a vowels is likely a place noun. The feminine ending ـة often appears on place nouns too: مَكْتَبَة (library), مَدْرَسَة (school).

cards.word: دَرَسَ (darasa) = he studied. Pattern: CaCaCa (فَعَلَ) — the standard Form I past tense verb pattern.
cards.grammarNote: The CaCaCa pattern (three short a vowels across three root consonants) is the most common Form I past tense shape. كَتَبَ (kataba, he wrote), دَرَسَ (darasa, he studied), عَمِلَ (ʿamila, he worked — slight variant with i on the second vowel).

cards.english: عَامِل (ʿāmil) means ___ and shares its pattern with ___
cards.word: عَامِل (ʿāmil) = worker/factor. CāCiC pattern — same as كَاتِب (kātib, writer) and دَارِس (dāris, studier).
cards.grammarNote: Root ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l) = work/doing. عَامِل is the active participle: long ā after ع, kasra under م. The CāCiC pattern reliably produces the 'doer' meaning across all roots.

cards.english: مُدَرِّس (mudarris) means ___ — why does it look different from دَارِس?
cards.word: مُدَرِّس (mudarris) = teacher. The doubled middle consonant (رّ) signals Form II — an intensive/causative form. A mudarris is one who causes others to study.
cards.grammarNote: Form II verbs double the middle root consonant and use the prefix مُـ in their active participle. مُدَرِّس (teacher) vs. دَارِس (studier/student). Form II often means 'to cause X' or 'to do X intensively,' so the doer is frequently a teacher, trainer, or professional.

cards.english: كُتُب (kutub) is the plural of كِتَاب. What type of plural is this?
cards.word: Broken plural (جمع التكسير, jamʿ al-taksīr) — the vowel pattern changes rather than adding a suffix. كِتَاب → كُتُب.
cards.grammarNote: Arabic often forms plurals by changing internal vowels rather than adding endings — these are called broken plurals. There are many patterns; CuCuC (كُتُب, كُتُب) is one common one. Broken plurals must often be memorised per word, but seeing the same root consonants tells you what the plural means.

cards.english: مَعْمَل (maʿmal) comes from root ___ and means ___
cards.word: Root ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l) = work/doing. مَعْمَل (maʿmal) = laboratory / factory — the place where work is done.
cards.grammarNote: maCCaC place-noun pattern at work again: م + ع-م-ل + short a vowels = a place of work. Same template as مَكْتَب (office, from writing root) and the implied place-nouns from dozens of other roots.

cards.english: You see an unfamiliar Arabic word. What is the first thing to look for?
cards.word: The 3-consonant root skeleton. Strip vowels and affixes (especially a leading م). Identify the three consonants in order — they point to the core meaning.
cards.grammarNote: Arabic has hundreds of roots. Once you know a root, you can often guess 8–10 related words. The patterns — CaCaCa (past verb), CāCiC (doer), maCCaC (place), maCCūC (passive), CiCāC (noun) — repeat across every root. Learn the patterns once; apply them everywhere.
أنا (ana) = I, used for both masculine and feminine speakers. In Arabic, the verb conjugation already encodes the subject, so أنا is often omitted in speech but used for emphasis.
Arabic distinguishes gender in 'you': أنتَ (anta) for masculine, أنتِ (anti) for feminine. The difference is a fatha (ـَ) vs kasra (ـِ) on the ت.
أنتِ (anti) = you (feminine). The kasra under the ت distinguishes it from أنتَ (anta = you, masculine). In unvowelled text they look identical — context and gender of the listener clarify.
هو (huwa) = he, and also 'it' for masculine nouns. Arabic has no neuter pronoun — every noun is masculine or feminine. الكتاب (the book) is masculine, so 'it' = هو.
هي (hiya) = she, and also 'it' for feminine nouns. الطاولة (the table) is feminine, so 'it' = هي.
نحن (nahnu) = we, used for both mixed and same-gender groups. The verb form for 'we' always begins with نـ (n-): نكتب (naktub = we write).
هم (hum) = they, for all-male or mixed-gender groups. The default plural pronoun. هن (hunna) is used for all-female groups.
Arabic has a special dual form for exactly two people or things. هما (huma) = the two of them. This is unique among major world languages. Dual also exists for nouns: كتابان (kitaban) = two books.
Equational sentence: no verb 'to be' in present tense. أنا (I) + طالب (student, masc.) = 'I am a student.' If the speaker is female: أنا طالبة (ana taaliba).
Arabic distinguishes masculine and feminine in 2nd person. anta (to a man), anti (to a woman).
The possessive suffix also changes: -ak (masc.) vs -ik (fem.). كيف حالك (to man) / كيف حالِك (to woman).
بخير (bikhyr) = well/fine. الحمد لله (al-hamdu lillah) = praise be to God — the standard positive response in Arabic.
ذَهَبَ (dhahaba) is the base form of the past tense — 3rd person masculine singular. The pattern فَعَلَ (fa'ala) with vowels a-a-a is the most common Form I past tense pattern.
Adding ـتْ (-at) to the base form creates the 3rd person feminine singular past. The taa' marbuta ت is written with sukuun (ـتْ) at the end of a sentence.
The 1st person singular past is formed by adding ـتُ (-tu) to the verb stem. The stem vowel drops: ذَهَبَ → ذَهَبْتُ.
The 1st person plural past is formed by adding ـنَا (-na) to the verb stem.
قَالَ (qala) is an irregular verb — it has a long vowel ā in the stem. The root is ق-و-ل. In 1st person: قُلْتُ (qultu), the long vowel shortens and the vowel changes.
قُلْتُ (qultu) shows the stem change in hollow verbs: the long ā shortens and the vowel changes to u when a consonant suffix is added.
فَعَلَ (fa'ala) = he did/made. This word is also the Arabic grammatical template verb — the root ف-ع-ل represents any generic verb root in grammar explanations.
جداً (jiddan) = very. It always follows the adjective: كبير جداً (very big), not جداً كبير. The ً is a tanwin sound (-an), always written with جداً.

cards.english: I am very happy to meet you.

cards.grammarNote: شكراً جزيلاً = thank you very much (literally: abundant thanks). جزيلاً is an alternative to جداً for intensifying certain expressions.
